newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-REED SEES FURTHER H2 STG HIT.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-REED SEES FURTHER H2 STG HIT.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch publisher Reed Elsvier said the strong pound wiped 36 million stg off its first half pre-tax profit and that the impact in the second half could be almost as great.

"Assuming sterling remains as strong the impact (in the second half) will be slightly lower than 36 million stg," Reed Elsevier co-chairman Nigel Stapleton told Reuters in a telephone interview, adding the effect would not be "substantially lower" than in the first half.
He said Reed Elsevier was prepared to spend a further two billion dollars on acquisition targets which met its financial and strategic criteria.

Stapleton said the company had been "comfortable" with reports earlier this year that it could spend up to three billion dollars on acquisitions and noted that it had since spent some one billion dollars.

"Growth by acquisition continues to be an important part of our strategic agenda...We are well up to speed with what might be available," Stapleton said, adding the company had identified targets that appeared to meet its criteria.
Reed Elsvier continues to look for opportunities in Europe after two relatively large U.S. deals in the first half. "We would like to do more in continental Europe," Stapleton said.
First half pre-tax profit rose only one percent to 419 million stg but Reed Elsevier said the increase would have been 10 percent at constant exchange rates.
The figure was at the bottom end of the forecast range and Reed shares fell 26p to 604p, a decline of four percent.
"The adjusting of forecasting for currencies tends to lag their actual movement and the impact is slightly larger than (analysts) expected," Stapleton said.
He said investment in initiatives in areas such as electronic publishing had trimmed growth by some two percent but noted that operating margins had improved by 0.5 percentage points.
Reed Elsevier said it planned to sell its remaining consumer book publishing activities -- comprising mainly of children's books and illustrated books.
Stapleton said the company was likely to sell the two parts separately. "We will take whichever route will deliver maximum value but it is more likely to be unbundled."
